title: Around the World in Eighty Days
author: Jules Verne
openingText: Mr. Phileas Fogg lived, in 1872, at No. 7, Saville Row, Burlington Gardens, the house in which Sheridan died in 1814. He was one of the most noticeable members of the Reform Club, though he seemed always to avoid attracting attention; an enigmatical personage, about whom little was known, except that he was a polished man of the world. He was never seen on 'Change, nor at the Bank, nor in the counting-rooms of the City; no ships ever came into London docks of which he was the owner; he had no public employment; he had never been entered at any of the Inns of Court; he had never pleaded either at the Chancery bar or the Queen's bench. He neither practised industry, nor trade, nor business of any sort. He belonged to the Reform, and that was all.
about:
Around the World in Eighty Days is the story of Phileas Fogg, an English gentleman of impeccable regularity, who wagers twenty thousand pounds at his club that he can circumnavigate the globe in eighty days. He leaves London that same evening with his new French manservant Passepartout, a one-way ticket to Dover, and no luggage worth speaking of. Following him from the first port is Detective Fix, who has mistaken Fogg for a bank robber and is determined to arrest him once he gets him back onto British soil. The chase takes them through Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, and New York — eighty days of ships, trains, elephants, and a burning funeral pyre from which Fogg rescues an Indian widow named Aouda, who travels with them to London. The wager is, in the end, won or lost by a margin of hours.

Verne serialized the novel in Le Temps from October 1872 and published it in book form the same year. He drew on Thomas Cook's actual tourist itineraries, contemporary railway timetables, and the completion of the transcontinental railroad (1869) and the Suez Canal (1869) to make the eighty-day figure credible — and tightly calibrated. The precision is the point. Fogg does not travel as an adventurer; he travels as a logistician, crossing the world as if the world were a problem in scheduling. Passepartout is the emotional center that Fogg refuses to be. Fix is the comic antagonist who pursues the wrong man across three continents. The book invented the race-against-the-clock narrative.

angleCards.title: The machine versus the world.
angleCards.text: Fogg treats the circumnavigation as a scheduling problem. The world keeps introducing the unexpected. The tension is between perfect planning and a planet that does not cooperate — and whether precision is a virtue or a refusal to be human.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the tension between Fogg's clockwork precision and the world's chaos — and ask what Verne thinks precision costs the person who carries it.

angleCards.title: What Passepartout sees.
angleCards.text: Fogg barely notices the places he passes through. Passepartout notices everything — the temples, the bazaars, the customs, the food. The circumnavigation looks completely different from the servant's perspective than from the master's.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the journey through Passepartout's eyes — his wonder, his improvisations, his disasters — as a counterweight to Fogg's abstraction.

angleCards.title: Fix and the law's limits.
angleCards.text: Detective Fix is right that a crime has been committed and wrong about who committed it. He pursues Fogg across three continents in perfect legal earnest. The comedy is about what happens when the machinery of law operates on false information.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Fix as a comic study in institutional error — a man doing his job correctly while pursuing the wrong conclusion, and what happens when the two things collide.

angleCards.title: Aouda — the passenger who stays.
angleCards.text: Fogg rescues Aouda from a funeral pyre in India. She is the only character who enters the story by choice rather than obligation, and she is the only one whose presence changes who Fogg is. She is not a trophy; she is the person the novel was secretly about.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Aouda and ask what she brings to the story — how the presence of a person with no stake in the wager changes what the wager is really about.

cast.name: Phileas Fogg
cast.description: Punctual, precise, taciturn, and entirely without apparent motive. He is independently wealthy, reads nothing, talks to no one, belongs only to the Reform Club, and passes his days in perfect routine: breakfast at the same hour, cards in the evening, retirement at midnight. He makes the wager on principle — because a man said it could not be done — and pursues it without emotion or deviation. The mystery of the novel is not whether he will win but whether he is a man at all, or a clock.

cast.name: Passepartout
cast.description: Jean Passepartout, former acrobat, fire-eater, and gymnastics teacher from Paris, who is hired by Fogg on the morning of the wager and departs with him that evening. He is everything Fogg is not: emotional, curious, easily surprised, capable of genuine delight and genuine fear. His improvisations — particularly in Bombay and San Francisco — are the reason the journey does not collapse. He is also the source of most of the disasters. He loves his master sincerely and cannot fathom him.

cast.name: Detective Fix
cast.description: A Scotland Yard detective who spots Fogg departing Suez and is convinced that Fogg matches the description of the man who robbed the Bank of England of fifty-five thousand pounds three days earlier. He is not entirely wrong in his method — he follows the evidence he has with professional diligence — but his evidence is wrong. He pursues Fogg across three continents, attempting to stall the journey long enough to receive his arrest warrant. He is the comic engine of the second half of the book: a man doing his job perfectly in the service of a completely false conclusion.

cast.name: Aouda
cast.description: A young Parsee widow whom Fogg rescues in India from a Brahmin funeral ceremony in which she was to be burned alongside her dead husband. She is educated, speaks English, and has relatives in Hong Kong who turn out to be inaccessible. She joins the circumnavigation by default and arrives in London with Fogg. She is the most fully human character in the novel — curious, grateful, and eventually in love with Fogg in a way that the book takes seriously rather than sentimentally.

cast.name: Sir Francis Cromarty
cast.description: A British general in India who shares a rail compartment with Fogg and Passepartout on the journey from Bombay to Calcutta. He is the one who explains the significance of the funeral procession and the risk of the rescue Fogg proposes. He is a reasonable, experienced man who considers the rescue reckless and assists with it anyway — one of those figures in Verne who represent competent adult judgment being overridden by a more radical kind of conviction.

cast.name: The Reform Club
cast.description: The gentlemen's club at Pall Mall where Fogg makes the wager on an October evening and to which he must return by the same date eighty days later. It is less a character than a structural principle: the place where precision is valued, where the wager is witnessed, and where the money waits. The club is the book's fixed point around which the world turns.

whyItMatters.title: The Race Against the Clock — Invented Here
whyItMatters.body: Around the World in Eighty Days invented the race-against-time narrative as a popular form. The thriller, the heist, the countdown — all of these owe something to Verne's construction of a journey whose entire tension is about margins. Fogg is not fleeing danger or pursuing a villain; he is fighting the calendar. Verne built the eighty-day figure from actual 1872 timetables, and the precision is central to the novel's effect: this is a world in which being twelve hours late matters, and the book makes the reader feel that fact in a way that earlier adventure fiction, with its vague timelines, did not. The structural innovation has been borrowed so many times that the original is easy to overlook.

whyItMatters.title: The New World and the Impassive Man
whyItMatters.body: Fogg crosses four continents in eighty days and notices almost none of them. Passepartout notices everything. The contrast between them is Verne's implicit argument about what industrialization and global connectivity were doing to the experience of the world: they were making it possible to travel everywhere and see nothing. Fogg is the figure of the new century — efficient, abstracted, indifferent to the specifics of any particular place. Passepartout is the older figure — a man for whom the world is full of particular and surprising things. The novel takes both seriously and does not resolve which mode of experiencing the world is better. That ambivalence is what keeps it alive.

whyItMatters.title: The Victorian World at Full Speed
whyItMatters.body: Verne wrote in 1872, three years after the completion of the Suez Canal and the American transcontinental railroad — both of which he incorporates into Fogg's itinerary. The book is a portrait of a specific technological moment: a world in which steam power had made global circumnavigation a matter of scheduling rather than adventure, and in which the British Empire had laid communication and transport infrastructure across enough of the surface that a meticulous man with money could plan a round trip in advance. Reading it in 2026, when a flight from London to Hong Kong takes thirteen hours, the eighty days feels distant — but Verne's point was never the time. It was the precision. The world he describes is one we still inhabit.

responses.theme: Who is Phileas Fogg — is he a real person?
responses.response:
Phileas Fogg is one of the stranger protagonists in nineteenth-century fiction, and Verne designed the strangeness deliberately. He is introduced as an enigma: a man who belongs to the Reform Club, follows a perfectly regular schedule, is wealthy with no apparent source of income, and has never been seen to feel anything. The question of whether he is a real person — whether there is a human being inside the precision — is the book's actual subject.

Verne gives you very little to work with. Fogg does not explain himself. He does not confide in Passepartout or Aouda or the reader. His internal states are almost entirely inaccessible: you see what he does, rarely what he feels. He proposes the circumnavigation without visible excitement. He crosses India without visible curiosity. He arrives in San Francisco without visible wonder. He rescues Aouda from a burning funeral pyre and then, on the same day, calculates whether the rescue has cost him enough time to affect the wager.

And yet the novel is clear that Fogg is not actually indifferent. He defends Passepartout at personal risk in San Francisco. He loans money to a stranger without being asked. He rescues Aouda when a rational calculating machine would have continued to the next train. At the end of the book, having lost the wager, he proposes to Aouda anyway — which is not the behavior of a man for whom the money was the point.

The most interesting reading of Fogg is not that he is a machine, but that he is a man who has made precision the discipline by which he manages a self that, if allowed to operate unchecked, would have a great deal more difficulty navigating the world. Passepartout is the id; Fogg is the superego; the journey tests which one the book can live without. The answer, which the ending provides, is neither — but the resolution arrives in one of the most understated final scenes in Victorian fiction, and it is worth not knowing it in advance.

responses.theme: How does Verne make the eighty days feel real?
responses.response:
Verne's method in Around the World in Eighty Days is journalism applied to fiction. He did not invent the itinerary; he researched it. The eighty-day figure comes from an actual 1872 article by Gaston Stiegler that compiled real transport timetables to calculate whether a circumnavigation in eighty days was theoretically possible. Verne used Thomas Cook's actual tourist packages and railway schedules to route Fogg's journey. The Suez Canal and the American transcontinental railroad — both completed in 1869 — are the technological advances that make the eighty days plausible where they had not been before.

This documentary precision is what gives the novel its distinctive texture. When Fogg's train from Bombay to Calcutta stops because the track runs out fifty miles short of Allahabad — a geographical fact Verne checked — the problem is not invented. When the route from San Francisco to New York takes seven days by train, that was the actual 1872 timetable. Verne was not writing future speculation; he was writing present capability. The world of 1872 could actually do this, just barely, and Verne wanted his readers to feel the barely.

The margin is the formal invention. Fogg's circumnavigation has almost no slack. Every delay — the rescue of Aouda, the imprisonment of Passepartout in Bombay, the storm off Japan — narrows the margin further. The reader is always calculating: how many days left, how many days behind, does this incident cost enough to matter? Verne makes this calculation easy by having his characters perform it explicitly and frequently. Fogg consults his itinerary. The reader consults the chapter heading. The eighty-day horizon is always visible.

The effect is different from modern thrillers, which tend to build tension through physical danger. Fogg is almost never in personal danger in any dramatic sense. The tension is logistical. You feel the compression of time, not the threat of death. This was new in 1872, and it produced a new kind of narrative anxiety — the anxiety of the schedule rather than the sword.

responses.theme: Verne and colonialism — what to do with the book's politics
responses.response:
Around the World in Eighty Days was published in 1872, at the height of European colonial confidence, and the book reflects that world with almost no critical distance. Fogg's route runs through British India, British Hong Kong, and American territories in the West — three of the main axes of European imperial expansion — and the local populations appear almost entirely as obstacles, scenery, or comic relief. The Indian funeral ceremony Fogg interrupts is presented as barbaric; the Chinese ports are exoticized; the American West is a landscape of adventure that happens to be populated by people who don't appear in the itinerary.

This is not a minor issue, and it is not something you can resolve by noticing that Verne includes Aouda as a sympathetic Indian character. Aouda is sympathetic because she is educated, speaks English, wears European clothes, and is being rescued from a practice Verne presents as self-evidently wrong. Her sympathy is conditional on her having already been assimilated to European norms. The Brahmin priests who conduct the funeral ceremony are not given a perspective.

The honest approach to the book's politics is to hold two things at once. First, the colonial assumptions are real and should be named — the book does not see the world it traverses; it sees a British itinerary running through territories whose people exist primarily as logistical variables. Second, Verne's actual argument is not straightforwardly about imperial superiority. His sympathies are with Passepartout, who is European but working-class, consistently bewildered, occasionally ridiculous, and the character the book treats most warmly. The Reform Club gentlemen who take the wager are not figures of admiration; they are men who believe they know how the world works and are proved wrong by an eccentricity they mistook for conformity.

Reading Verne in 2026 means reading a book that was written in good faith by a man who could not see what he could not see, and that contains, within its colonial frame, a genuine argument about precision, regularity, and the cost of treating the world as a scheduling problem. Both things are true at once. The book repays attention to what it sees and to what it is unable to imagine seeing.

preReadingChat.fallback: Around the World in Eighty Days is the book that invented the race-against-the-clock narrative — a journey from London to London in exactly eighty days, calculated to the hour using real 1872 timetables, powered by steam and the British gentleman's faith in precision. Fogg is the puzzle: a man who may or may not be fully human. Passepartout is the heart. Fix is the comedy. Aouda is the reason the wager turns out to be about something other than the money. Ask me about any of them before you start.
